parts.problemMd: Do you think a business being ethical will always lead to lower profits? **Justify **your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Some customers may be prepared to pay extra for ethical products or ethical company behaviour** [K]**. This can help offset the increased costs of using ethically-sourced materials, for example, **[An]** so overall profit margin may not change**,** and the better reputation gained could result in additional sales** [An]**

However, some firms may struggle to find ethically-sourced raw materials, especially locally** [K]**. The long delivery distances and extra transport costs **[An]** may push prices so high that demand is reduced** [An]** and profits fall

Therefore, being ethical can benefit a business, as in the long term revenue** **and profits may increase ** [E]**. However, some customers may not be prepared to pay the higher price for the ethical behaviour, particularly for everyday low-cost items **[E] **so profits are likely to fall

Therefore, being ethical can benefit a business as in the long term this may increase revenue [eval] which could result in higher profit overall [eval]

parts.problemMd: Do you think businesses should prioritise ethical practices over profit maximisation? **Justify** your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Businesses may prioritise profit maximisation over ethical practices because ethical sourcing and fair labour practices require higher operational costs **[K]**. This reduces profit margins and may make products less competitive on price **[An]**

However, businesses that ignore ethical practices risk facing consumer boycotts **[K]**, as customers increasingly demand transparency and ethical behaviour from companies. This could lead to significant revenue losses and damaged brand reputation **[An]**

Businesses should consider that whilst prioritising profit may provide short-term financial gains, unethical practices can result in legal penalties and regulatory sanctions **[E]**. Furthermore, companies that maintain strong ethical standards often build greater customer loyalty and attract socially conscious investors, ultimately creating sustainable long-term profitability **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:** **MainCity Bakery (MB)** MainCity Bakery (MB) MB is a small bakery that produces bread. Yasin started the bakery 6 months ago with help from the government. Yasin needed a business plan to support his application for government help. An extract from the business plan Yasin produced is shown in Appendix 1. The market research was carried out by Yasin. He asked a small sample of family and friends to fill in a questionnaire. Yasin’s business plan also contained forecast data. MB’s bread is freshly-made every day in the bakery, which is located at the back of MB’s small shop. The bread is then sold the same day. Yasin has 2 employees to help him produce the bread and 1 employee to serve customers in the shop. All employees work 5 days a week and are paid the legal minimum wage. Yasin uses a democratic leadership style. Yasin needs to keep costs low to be competitive. He uses packaging that cannot be recycled. Yasin also buys the cheapest ingredients, most of which are imported. He is planning to use lean production in the bakery but he has to decide which method to use. MB’s main competitors advertise that they only use ingredients from local suppliers. Yasin is thinking of changing the suppliers he uses for ingredients and packaging. He wants MB to have a good ethical image which he could use in advertising. Yasin plans to start making cakes. He is considering two options as outlined in Appendix 2. MB’s fixed costs will increase as there will be additional expenses whichever option he chooses. **Appendix 1 ** **Extract from Yasin’s business plan for MB** | Section | Details | |---|---| | Market research | Questionnaire results are as follows:

- Bread is eaten by all age groups
- Of the sample asked:
- 85% want products made using ingredients from local suppliers
- 70% want to purchase cakes as well as bread from a bakery | | Resources | - \$10 000 to buy bakery equipment
- Rent for the bakery and shop each month
- \$3000 for start-up supplies and ingredients | **Appendix 2** **Forecast data for MB’s cake options** | | **Option 1 Small cupcakes** | **Option 2 Large birthday cakes** | |---|---|---| | Monthly sales of cakes | 4000 | 100 | | Variable cost per cake | \$0.50 | \$10 | | Additional fixed cost per month | \$3000 | \$3000 | | Price per cake | \$2 per cupcake | \$60 per birthday cake | | Gross profit margin | 75% | 83.33% | | Sales growth | Low | High | **Appendix 3 ** **Packaging supplier advertisement** We only supply packaging made from sustainable sources. This will keep your products fresh and protect the environment. We can deliver your packaging when you need it. Consider the following **three **ways Yasin could improve the ethical image of MB. - Buying all ingredients from local suppliers. - Using only environmentally friendly packaging. - Increasing wage rates to 20% above the legal minimum wage. Which way would be most effective? **Justify **your answer. Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/jun-2022-paper-2-case-study---new.pdf)when answering the question
parts.solutionMd:
By switching to local suppliers, MB could compete directly with rivals on their ethical stance. It aligns with Yasin's desire to develop an ethical image **[Ap]** and, as 85% of people surveyed want products made using local ingredients **[Ap]**,  it would be very popular with customers and could significantly boost MB's image and sales. It is likely, though, to be more expensive than buying cheaper, imported ingredients **[An]**

Currently, MB uses packaging that cannot be recycled **[Ap]**, which is not sustainable. Switching to eco-friendly packaging would reduce waste and appeal to environmentally conscious customers **[An]**, and there is an available supplier of sustainable packaging **[Ap]**. However, this might increase costs and some customers may not notice the change in packaging **[An]**

Increasing wages to 20% above the legal minimum could improve employee motivation and reduce staff turnover within the bakery **[Ap]**. This could lead to better quality products, indirectly improving MB's image **[An]**. However, it would increase costs significantly and may not be as visible to customers as the other options **[An]**

Overall, the improved ethical image and ability to compete with local rivals on social responsibility could justify the higher costs of local ingredients **[E]**. Sourcing locally offers the best balance of meeting customer preferences, matching competitor strategies, and creating a visible ethical stance **[**`equation`E**]** for customers of bakery products** [Ap]**. This approach is most likely to enhance MB's reputation and attract environmentally conscious customers than the other options **[**`equation`E**]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Buying all ingredients from local suppliers**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Ingredients sourced locally → no imports → lower transport pollution and carbon footprint
>     - Supports local businesses (e.g. flour mills) → strengthens community relations
>     - Cheaper and quicker deliveries → fresher ingredients and lower logistics cost
>     - Meets customer demand (85 % surveyed prefer local sourcing) → aligns with market preferences
>     - Matches competitor practices → no loss of competitive position
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Local ingredients cost more than low-cost imports → may require higher selling prices → risk of reduced demand
>     - Limited supplier range → potential constraints on product variety and recipe flexibility
> - **Using only environmentally friendly packaging**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Enhances bakery’s green image → appeals to eco-aware consumers and new market segments
>     - Future-proofs against stricter environmental regulations → reduces compliance risk
>     - Reliable sustainable packaging supplier available (Appendix 3) → ensures continuity
>     - Lowers risk of activist or pressure-group backlash → protects reputation
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Eco-friendly packaging may offer less product protection → risk of damaged goods
>     - Time spent sourcing new packaging → less focus on core baking operations
>     - Higher packaging costs (likely 10 %+ increase) → may force price hikes → some customers may resist
> - **Increasing wages to 20 % above the legal minimum**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Better pay → higher employee motivation and productivity
>     - Lower staff turnover → savings on recruitment and training
>     - Stronger employer brand → easier to attract and retain quality workers
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Wage bill increases → higher operating costs → profit margins under pressure
>     - If competitors match pay rises → loses motivational advantage
>     - Pay policy may not be widely known → limited impact on public reputation
> - **Recommendation**
> 
>   - Local sourcing delivers environmental and community benefits but needs a pricing or volume strategy to offset higher input costs
>   - Sustainable packaging boosts the bakery’s green credentials and regulatory resilience yet demands careful cost management to retain price competitiveness
>   - Above-minimum wages foster staff loyalty and productivity but should be clearly communicated to amplify reputational gains without eroding margins

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

**Cell Covers (CC) **

Aisha worked for several years for a company that repairs mobile (cell) phones in country Z. She had always wanted to be her own boss and decided to leave her job to set up CC to produce covers for mobile phones. She went into partnership with her brother, Aruna. He worked as an Operations Manager for a company producing children’s clothes.

The sources of finance for the business were \$10 000 of savings from each partner and a bank loan of \$10 000. CC was also given a government grant to help the new business get started. CC leased a factory, bought some equipment and had to pay some expenses before the business had regular cash inflows.

CC’s current product is a range of standardised phone covers which are sold in the mass market. These are sold using a competitive pricing method through mobile phone shops. CC employs 10 skilled production workers who are paid just above the legal minimum wage. These workers have been trained how to operate the equipment and work as a team on the production line. During the production process there is a lot of waste plastic produced and CC sends this to landfill sites. The business has just completed its second year of trading.

CC is about to launch a new range of individual personalised phone covers. It will need to recruit 2 additional production workers. Aruna knows that the marketing mix for this new product may have to be different to the marketing mix used for the standardised products. The new product will be aimed at a niche market of high income consumers between the ages of 18 to 25. There are few other competitors in this market at present.

**Appendix 1 **

**Newspaper article in Main News **

Country Z has been in a recession but the economy is now growing rapidly and unemployment is falling. With higher incomes the majority of people now own a mobile phone. This makes communication easier. Mobile banking is becoming more popular and it is used by a large percentage of the population.

**Appendix 2 **

**Advertisement for CC’s standardised mobile phone covers**

Do you want to protect your phone from damage? Then buy a phone cover from CC. Your phone will never be damaged if you use one of our high quality covers!!

We offer a range of standardised covers at competitive prices. The CC range has many different colours and designs so you will stand out from the crowd.

**Appendix 3 **

**Summary of CC’s financial information from the end of the second year of trading (\$)**

| Revenue | 800 000 |
|---|---|
| Cost of sales | 400 000 |
| Gross profit | 400 000 |
| Expenses | 250 000 |
| Profit | 150 000 |
| Current Assets | 20 000 |
| of which: Inventory | 5 000 |
| Current liabilities | 15 000 |

Consider how the changes in the following **three **government legal controls could affect CC.

- Increase in the minimum wage
- More controls over what can be stated in advertisements
- No waste plastic can be sent to landfill sites

Which change is likely to have the greatest effect on profit? **Justify **your answer.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/nov-2020-paper-22-case-study-v2---new.pdf)when answering the question
parts.solutionMd:
An increase in the minimum wage would likely raise CC's costs, as they currently pay their 10 skilled production workers just above the minimum wage **[Ap]**. With plans to hire two additional workers for their new personalised covers **[Ap]**, this could further increase labour costs. CC might need to raise prices or find ways to increase productivity to maintain profits **[An]**

More controls over claims made in advertising could impact CC's marketing strategy. Their current advertisement states, "Your phone will never be damaged if you use one of our high quality covers!!"**[Ap]** If this claim is found to be misleading, CC may need to change their advertising approach, which could incur costs for market research **[An]**

The ban on sending waste plastic to landfill sites would require CC to find alternative methods of disposing of the large amount of plastic waste **[Ap]** it generates. However, recycling this waste could significantly increase their costs because it may involve investing in new equipment or outsourcing to specialist recycling companies **[An]**

The ban on sending waste plastic to landfill sites is likely to have the greatest effect on profit **[E]**. It would require a complete overhaul of CC's waste management processes, affecting both their standardised covers and new personalised range **[Ap]**. While the other changes are significant, they may be easier to adapt to through gradual wage increases or changing marketing strategies **[E]**. The waste management issue, however, affects all of CC's production process and would require immediate and costly solutions **[E]**

SSM is a public limited company that was set up 25 years ago. SSM manufacture soap powder in country Y. The soap powder is used for washing clothes. SSM has a total of 100 employees with 60 in the Operations Department. It uses flow production in the factory and has 10 production lines with 5 workers and 1 supervisor for each line. The Operations Manager is aware that production workers are unhappy and often complain about their jobs being boring. These workers have always been paid by an hourly rate. The Human Resources Manager has recommended changes to ensure fewer workers leave each year to work for other businesses.

The directors of SSM have decided to expand the factory. They will need \$15m to do this. The directors have also considered taking over a competitor. SSM is likely to benefit from economies of scale as it grows.

The Marketing Director thinks SSM should start selling soap powder in markets in other countries. SSM will need to carry out either primary market research or secondary market research to forecast the potential total sales in these new markets. There are many existing manufacturers in these countries. SSM need to consider the problems when entering new markets in other countries such as tariffs or quotas.

**Appendix 1**

** Manufacturing process to make soap powder**

All the different types of soap powder are manufactured on production lines using flow production. SSM makes use of specialisation.

Each production line has the following stages:

Each of these stages uses machinery controlled by a production worker.

**Appendix 2 **

**Email from the SSM Finance Director to the Managing Director**

SSM has a cash-flow problem which may get worse. Please see charts below.

**Appendix 3 **

**Newspaper article from Main News 1 October 2021 **

Retailers have reported increased sales for most types of products such as sales of washing machines which have increased by 15%. Economic growth in country Y is predicted to increase.

Many businesses have been recruiting additional employees and there are now shortages of some skilled workers. The government in country Y has recorded an increase in inflation to 8% so far this year, which is a worry.

- Cultural differences
- Lack of knowledge
- Import restrictions

Which problem is likely to have the most effect on SSM? **Justify **your answer.

parts.solutionMd:
Cultural differences could pose issues for SSM, as soap powder preferences may vary between countries. SSM currently only sells to large retailers in country Y **[Ap]**. In new markets, consumers may prefer different scents **[Ap]**, packaging or product features that SSM is not familiar with. This could require costly product development to make adaptations **[An]**

Import restrictions like tariffs or quotas would increase costs or limit how much soap powder SSM could sell abroad. This would make it harder for SSM to compete on price with local manufacturers, especially with inflation rising **[Ap]** or sell in high enough volumes to achieve economies of scale **[An]**

SSM has no experience selling outside country Y **[Ap]**, so they lack understanding of consumer preferences, competitors, and distribution channels in foreign markets. There are many existing manufacturers in potential new countries **[Ap]**. Without knowledge of these rivals' products, prices and market positioning, SSM would struggle to develop effective marketing strategies. They may also face challenges establishing relationships with new retailers or distributors **[An]**

Of the three problems listed, lack of knowledge is likely to have the greatest effect on SSM's expansion plans **[E]**. While SSM could conduct market research to gain knowledge **[Ap]**, this is expensive and time-consuming. Cultural differences and import restrictions are more easily addressed once SSM understands the new soap powder **[Ap]**market **[E]**. Therefore, lack of knowledge is likely to have the most significant impact on SSM's international expansion plans **[E]**

**Sports Safety Equipment (SSE)**

SSE manufactures sports safety equipment in country Z. It is a public limited company which has been successful for over 30 years. The main product SSE manufactures is safety helmets for different sports, such as bicycle riding, cricket and skateboarding. SSE has one large factory making the safety helmets. The factory uses flow production. The production workers each specialise in one task on the production line. SSE’s raw materials are imported.

SSE sells its helmets in several other countries and is planning to expand into many more. It will need to carry out market research before entering new markets in other countries. Each country has different sports that are popular and the style of helmets varies from country to country.

SSE plans to build its own factories in its most important markets in other countries and will need to choose a suitable source of finance. The Human Resources Director has decided to use internal recruitment for the managers of the new factories. There will need to be effective communication between the managers of the new factories and SSE’s head office in country Z.

Most of SSE’s sales in country Z are through sports equipment shops. Customers like to try on the helmets to check they fit correctly. SSE currently sells its helmets in other countries through its website.

SSE is also increasing its product range. The latest new product being developed is a children’s cricket helmet. A break-even chart for this new product is shown in Appendix 3.

**Appendix 1 **

**Extract from SSE’s website **

**If you want the best protection when playing sport then buy an SSE safety helmet!**

We supply a wide range of safety helmets for you when playing sport.

Whatever the sport - SSE produces a helmet for you.

You can order directly from this website by entering your head measurements below.

Get the perfect fit for you!

**Appendix 2 **

**Email from SSE’s Managing Director to SSE’s Finance Director**

To: Finance Director

From: Managing Director

Date: 1 September 2023

Re: Demand for SSE’s products Demand for SSE’s products in country Z is forecast to increase. Our government has imposed import tariffs on safety helmets. We may be able to increase our prices.

The exchange rate in country Z is expected to fall. However, other countries have introduced import quotas on safety helmets.

We will have to consider all the likely effects of these changes.

**Appendix 3 **

**Projected weekly break-even chart for SSE’s new children’s cricket helmet**

The maximum output and sales for this product is 1000 units per week.

Consider how each of the following **three **changes may affect SSE.

- A depreciation in the currency of country Z
- An import tariff introduced on sports helmets imported into country Z
- Quotas introduced on sports helmets in countries where SSE sells its products

Which change is likely to have the greatest effect on SSE’s profit? **Justify **your answer.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/nov-2023-paper-2-case-study-v2---new.pdf)when answering the question
parts.solutionMd:
A depreciation in country Z's currency would make SSE's exports of children's cricket helmets **[Ap] **cheaper and more competitive in other countries. This could increase sales and revenue from exports **[An]**. However, SSE's imported raw materials **[Ap] **would become more expensive, increasing costs **[An]**

An import tariff on sports helmets into country Z would make imported helmets more expensive compared to SSE's domestically-produced helmets **[Ap] **. This could allow SSE to increase its prices and market share in country Z, potentially boosting profits on sales there **[An]**

Quotas on sports helmet imports in SSE's export markets would limit the quantity of helmets SSE could sell in those countries. This may reduce SSE's sales and revenue from exports **[An]**. SSE plans to build its own factories in its most important markets in other countries **[Ap]**, which could be a way to bypass these quotas.

The depreciation of country Z's currency is likely to have the greatest effect on SSE's profit **[E] **. As SSE sells helmets in several other countries and plans to expand into many more **[Ap]**, the increased competitiveness of its exports could substantially boost sales volumes and revenue. While import costs would rise, the potential for significantly higher export sales could outweigh this, leading to the largest impact on overall profitability compared to the other changes **[E] **

> NSN is a multinational company. It makes cars. Over the years, technology has changed production methods. NSN uses just-in-time inventory control in all its factories. NSN plans to open a new factory in country Z creating 7,000 jobs. Country Z’s Government has offered an \$80m grant to NSN. A spokesperson for NSN said: ‘Governments should support business activity. There were also other factors that influenced our decision to build the new factory there including the possible effects of economic growth.’

**Explain two **ways in which an increase in economic growth might affect NSN’s decision to build a new factory in country Z.
parts.solutionMd:
An increase in economic growth could lead to increased demand **[K]** for NSN's cars **[Ap],** which would lead to an increase in sales revenue and, potentially, profit** [An]**

However, economic growth may lead to a shortage of skilled workers **[K]**. This may make it more difficult for NSN to recruit workers **[An]** to fill the 7,000 jobs in its new factory** [Ap]**

parts.problemMd: Do you think a reduction in the level of unemployment always benefits businesses? **Justify **your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
A reduction in the level of unemployment means more people have jobs and an income** [K]**. This may mean businesses experience more sales, leading to higher potential revenue **[An]**

However, because there are fewer people looking for work, it may be difficult to recruit workers **[K]**. This could make it difficult to increase output to meet the higher demand** [An]**

Overall, it may depend on whether the business currently has unfilled vacancies or not** [E]**. Without being able to recruit new  workers, they may not be able to produce enough to benefit from higher potential sales** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - You are writing a mini-argument with a decision
> 
>   - Give one relevant reason to support your view → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this reason helps the business (cause-effect chain) →  1 An mark
>   - Give a different possible reason or viewpoint → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this could also help the business → 1 An mark
>   - Make a decision — which argument is stronger or more important overall? → up to 2 E marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Increase in sales [k] could lead to higher revenue [an]
>   - Difficult to recruit workers [k] which may lead to an increase in recruitment costs / difficult to increase output / meet orders [an]
>   - Higher wages may need to be paid [k] increasing labour costs [an]
>   - Available workers may lack necessary skills [k] leading to lower productivity / higher training costs / lower quality [an]
>   - Other appropriate responses should also be credited
> - Justification might include:
> 
>   - A reduction in unemployment may mean more sales [k] leading to higher potential revenue [an]. However, because there are fewer people looking for work it may be difficult to recruit workers [k] which could make it difficult to increase output [an]. Overall, it may depend on whether the business needs employees or not, as without sufficient workers they may not be able to produce enough to benefit from higher potential sales [eval] [eval]

parts.problemMd: Do you think all businesses benefit from an increase in government spending? **Justify **your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
An increase in government spending would mean more money is being pumped into the economy **[K]**. This could mean there are more jobs and more workers with income**, **which could lead to an increase in sales **[An]**

However, in order to pay for the higher government spending, a rise in taxes **[K] **may be needed.  This will lead to an increase in costs, which in turn could lead to businesses having to set higher prices to cover them **[An]**

Overall, I think all businesses can benefit. For example, if the government decides to build new roads, construction businesses are likely to benefit the most **[E] **as they can receive an increase in revenue from the extra sales. However, other businesses can still benefit from better transport links, which can help all businesses send or receive goods on time** [E]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

**Safari Adventures (SA) **

Tokumbo is a sole trader. He started SA 2 years ago in country X. Tokumbo had previously worked for a company selling holidays. SA organises safari tours which take tourists to view wild animals on a game reserve. Most of SA’s customers are tourists from other countries. Tokumbo did not have any objectives when he started SA but knows they are important for his business.

SA uses its own vehicles for the 7 day safari tours and provides accommodation in small local hotels. Tokumbo employs 4 safari guides, 1 for each of the 4 vehicles. The safari guides drive the tourists around the game reserve. There is 1 additional employee who helps Tokumbo in the office with administration. Tokumbo thinks SA needs a website so tourists can book directly with them rather than booking through holiday companies that charge SA a fee.

Tokumbo is considering the following three options for the future growth of SA safari tours:

- Option 1 - increasing the number of safari guides and vehicles to increase the number of customers from the existing target market
- Option 2 – targeting young people who want to camp and sleep in a tent on their safari
- Option 3 - targeting high-income tourists who prefer to stay in luxury hotels

Information about these three options is outlined in Appendix 3.

Tokumbo plans to provide more training for his employees whichever option he chooses. He wants his existing employees to have a wider knowledge of the wild animals on the game reserve and to be able to provide high-quality customer service. Tokumbo has to decide which method of training to use.

**Appendix 1 **

**Newspaper article in Main News, September 2022 **

**Tourism takes off**

Country X is becoming a popular holiday destination for tourists from other countries.

There is an increased demand from high-income tourists who want to stay in luxury hotels whilst on safari tours. These tourists are willing to pay high prices. There is also a new trend for younger people who want cheaper holidays. They prefer to camp and sleep in tents on game reserves rather than stay in hotels.

Are the many safari businesses in country X ready to target these new markets?

The use of e-commerce to find and book safari tours by tourists from other countries is offering both opportunities and threats to businesses in country X.

The inflation rate in country X has increased to 4% which may affect some of our local safari businesses.

**Appendix 2 **

**Email from Tokumbo’s accountant**

To: Tokumbo

From: Accountant

Subject: Source of finance for the new vehicles

New vehicles will be needed whichever option you choose for the future growth of your business.

I have considered several sources of finance you could use for the new vehicles. Interest rates on bank loans have fallen to 2% whilst interest rates on savings are 3%. I think you should choose from one of the following sources:

- Leasing
- Bank loan
- Retained profit

We can meet to discuss these sources if that would help you to decide.

**Appendix 3 **

**SA’s three options for a 7 day safari tour**

|   | Option 1 More existing safari tours | Option 2 Camping safari tours | Option 3 Luxury safari tours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forecast number of tourists per week | 16 | 32 | 10 |
| Total costs per week for SA to provide these safari tours | \$12 000 | \$8000 | \$20 000 |
| Average cost per tourist | \$750 | ? | ? |
| Price per tourist | \$1000 | \$400 | \$2400 |

Explain **two **possible effects on SA of the increase in the rate of inflation in country X.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/nov-2022-paper-21-case-study---new.pdf)when answering the question
parts.solutionMd:
If there is inflation of 4% **[Ap]**, then prices of basic goods may be increasing significantly in country X** [K]**. This will mean there is more pressure on SA to increase the wages of employees **[An]** because employees cannot maintain their standard of living without a wage increase **[An]**

Inflation is likely to cause a rise in prices for safari tours** [K]**. This could lead to a decrease in demand** [An]** as it will be harder to attract tourists to country X  **[Ap]**. This means SA will suffer a  decrease in revenue as demand for safari tours is likely to be price elastic** [An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Write two full paragraphs, one for each reason/point
> - In each paragraph:
> 
>   - State one valid point relevant to the question → 1 K mark
>   - Apply it clearly to the case study → 1 Ap mark
>   - Explain how it works using a cause–effect chain → up to 2 An marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Relevant answers might include:
> 
>   - Likely rise in prices for safari tours – decreased demand / harder to attract tourists to country X – decreased revenue for SA if demand is price elastic – possible decrease in profits if costs rise more than revenue
>   - Increase in costs for SA – may need to spend time sourcing lower cost inputs / updating the brochures – keep recalculating prices / need to keep printing brochures with new prices
>   - More pressure to increase wages for SA employees – prices of basic goods may be increasing significantly in country X – as employees cannot maintain their standard of living without a wage increase – increases costs
>   - Increased cost of investment / equipment – may mean expansion is delayed
> - Application could include:
> 
>   - Safari holidays; increase in tourists from other countries; high income tourists; luxury safari holidays; 5 employees; only been operating for 2 years; sole trader; game reserve; camping / tent; wild animals; 4 safari guides; 4 safari vehicles; accommodation in local / luxury hotels; fuel

**Extract:**

**Gemma’s Jewels (GJ)**

Gemma set up GJ as a sole trader 5 years ago in country Z. She started by selling rings and bracelets from a rented shop. She used her own savings to start the business. The first year was successful. After this first year Gemma decided to expand by selling more expensive items of jewellery. Gemma thinks it is important to set clear business objectives. She wants her business to increase sales by 10% each year and to increase market share.

As the business grew Gemma needed more finance for a computer, inventory and working capital to avoid liquidity problems. She decided to convert the business to a private limited company and sell shares to members of her family. Gemma still owns more than 50% of the shares in GJ.

In 2019, Gemma purchased a franchise from Beautywise Jewellery. This means GJ is now only able to sell Beautywise products in its shop. GJ has to purchase all of its inventory from Beautywise and in addition pay 20% of gross profit to Beautywise. More details about the franchise are in the advertisement in Appendix 1.

Gemma has developed a website so customers can order online. Customers can also download a mobile (cell) phone app to view and order jewellery.

Gemma plans to open a second shop as a Beautywise franchise in a nearby town. She has to decide which method of sales promotion to use. GJ needs to recruit a manager for the new shop. The manager will be responsible for operating the shop and making most of the decisions about which items of inventory to buy. The manager will also need to ensure excellent customer service is provided and that the new employees are motivated and working efficiently.

**Appendix 1 **

**Advertisement for Beautywise Jewellery Franchise**

**Become a franchisee to sell Beautywise Jewellery and improve your chances of success!!**

What we offer you:

- Be the only shop in your area that sells Beautywise jewellery
- Beautywise will advertise nationally on television and in newspapers
- Help and advice on decoration of the shop and training for employees and the franchisee
- Ethically sourced jewellery imported especially for Beautywise
- The franchise fee is just \$50 000 per year!

**Appendix 2 **

**Newspaper article- Daily News **

**External factors affecting the jewellery market in country Z**

The demand for jewellery in country Z is likely to be affected by some recent changes. Consumers are becoming more aware of the ethical issues involved in jewellery production in some countries. The exchange rate of the currency of country Z is likely to depreciate over the next 12 months. The Government is planning changes to tax rates which might reduce the effects of the current economic boom.

**Appendix 3 **

**Information on three possible locations for the new shop**

| **Annual costs** | **Town A** | **Town B** | **Town C** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shop rent | \$45 000 per year for 5 years | \$35 000 per year for 10 years | \$20 000 per year for 15 years |
| Wages and salaries | \$80 000 | \$70 000 | \$60 000 |
| Heating and lighting | \$5 000 | \$5 000 | \$3 000 |
| Estimated gross profit | \$400 000 | \$300 000 | \$200 000 |

Note: Franchise fee is \$50 000 per year and 20% of gross profit is paid to Beautywise.

Consider how the following **three **changes might affect GJ.

- All jewellery packaging must state in which country the product has been made
- Country Z has entered a boom phase of the business cycle
- A higher percentage of people in country Z use mobile (cell) phones

Which change is likely to have the most effect on GJ’s profit? **Justify **your answer.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/nov-2020-paper-2-case-study---new.pdf)when answering the question
parts.solutionMd:
The requirement to state the country of origin on jewellery packaging may benefit GJ. It sells ethically sourced jewellery,  imported by Beautywise **[Ap]**. Highlighting this could improve GJ's reputation and attract customers who care about ethical sourcing, potentially increasing sales and profit **[An]**

The economic boom in Country Z will likely have a significant positive impact on GJ's profit. GJ sells expensive jewellery items **[Ap]**. During a boom, consumers have higher incomes and are more willing to spend on luxury goods like jewellery. This could substantially increase GJ's sales and profit margins **[An]**

The increased use of mobile phones in Country Z also presents an opportunity for GJ. GJ has developed a website and mobile app for customers to view and order jewellery **[Ap]**. With more people using mobile phones, GJ can reach a wider audience through its app, potentially increasing online sales and profit **[An]**

The economic boom will have the greatest effect on profit **[E]**. Jewellery is a luxury good, so increased consumer income during a boom should drive substantial sales growth **[E] **across all of GJ's product lines and sales channels, including its website and mobile app **[Ap]**. This broad increase in demand is likely to outweigh the more specific impacts of the other two changes **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Packaging country of origin labelling**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - May boost GJ’s ethical reputation → customers see franchise as sourcing responsibly → stronger brand trust
>     - Differentiates GJ jewellery in a crowded market → appeals to ethically minded buyers
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Many shoppers care more about style and price → origin label may go unnoticed
>     - Adds packaging cost and complexity → minimal sales uplift if ethics not a priority
> - **Country Z entering an economic boom**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Rising incomes → more disposable cash for luxury items → higher jewellery sales
>     - Opportunity to raise prices without deterring buyers → improves margins
>     - Higher-quality positioning pays off → affluent customers upgrade to GJ
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Jewellery buying often tied to special occasions (weddings, birthdays) → boom effect may be uneven
>     - Consumers may first spend on other big-ticket goods → jewellery sales could lag
> - **Higher mobile-phone usage in Country Z**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Easier access to GJ’s website and app → online browsing and purchasing → wider reach beyond shop locale
>     - Enables targeted social-media advertising → low-cost, high-engagement marketing
>     - Opens export opportunities → sales to customers overseas without physical stores
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Added delivery and return costs → cuts into profit margins
>     - Some customers still prefer in-store try-on → online alone may limit sales
>     - Greater online visibility → tougher digital competition
> - **Conclusion**
> 
>   - Economic boom likely drives the biggest profit uplift via higher incomes and price leverage
>   - Mobile-phone adoption can deliver the greatest sales growth if GJ executes strong digital marketing and controls fulfilment costs
>   - Ethical packaging strengthens brand loyalty among conscious consumers but has smaller overall impact unless ethics are a key purchase driver
>   - GJ should prioritise pricing and product availability to capture boom spending, then invest in digital channels, using origin labelling as a brand enhancement for the right audience

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

**Soapy Sudds Manufacturer (SSM) **

SSM is a public limited company that was set up 25 years ago. SSM manufacture soap powder in country Y. The soap powder is used for washing clothes. SSM sells all its soap powder to large retailers in country Y. SSM’s sales have been increasing for many years in country Y but sales in the last year have remained the same. The directors of SSM are considering ways to increase sales.

SSM has a total of 100 employees with 60 in the Operations Department. It uses flow production in the factory and has 10 production lines with 5 workers and 1 supervisor for each line. The Operations Manager is aware that production workers are unhappy and often complain about their jobs being boring. These workers have always been paid by an hourly rate. The Human Resources Manager has recommended changes to ensure fewer workers leave each year to work for other businesses.

The directors of SSM have decided to expand the factory. They will need \$15m to do this. The directors have also considered taking over a competitor. SSM is likely to benefit from economies of scale as it grows.

The Marketing Director thinks SSM should start selling soap powder in markets in other countries. SSM will need to carry out either primary market research or secondary market research to forecast the potential total sales in these new markets. There are many existing manufacturers in these countries. SSM need to consider the problems when entering new markets in other countries such as tariffs or quotas.

**Appendix 1**

** Manufacturing process to make soap powder**

All the different types of soap powder are manufactured on production lines using flow production. SSM makes use of specialisation.

Each production line has the following stages:

Each of these stages uses machinery controlled by a production worker.

**Appendix 2 **

**Email from the SSM Finance Director to the Managing Director**

SSM has a cash-flow problem which may get worse. Please see charts below.

**Appendix 3 **

**Newspaper article from Main News 1 October 2021 **

Retailers have reported increased sales for most types of products such as sales of washing machines which have increased by 15%. Economic growth in country Y is predicted to increase.

Many businesses have been recruiting additional employees and there are now shortages of some skilled workers. The government in country Y has recorded an increase in inflation to 8% so far this year, which is a worry.

Consider the effects on SSM of the following changes in country Y:

- Increase in employment
- Increase in inflation

Which effect is likely to have the greatest impact on SSM’s profit? **Justify **your answer.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/nov-2021-paper-2-case-study---new.pdf)when answering the question
parts.solutionMd:
An increase in employment is likely to mean that disposable incomes will rise, potentially increasing demand for SSM's soap powder. Sales of washing machines have increased by 15%, which suggests higher demand for complementary products like soap powder **[Ap]**. This could allow SSM to increase sales and revenue. However, the labour market shortage mentioned may force SSM to raise wages to attract and retain workers, increasing costs **[An]**

Higher inflation of 8% will increase SSM's costs for raw materials and SSM's workers may demand higher wages to offset rising living costs. It may need to raise prices to maintain its profit margins **[An]**. This could reduce demand if consumers become more price sensitive. As SSM's sales have remained static recently **[Ap]**, raising prices could further hurt sales and SSM's ability to make a profit **[An]**

Overall, the increase in inflation is likely to have the greatest impact on SSM's profit **[E]**. While higher employment may boost demand, the significant 8% inflation rate will squeeze SSM's profit margins for several reasons, including higher costs and lower sales of washing powder **[Ap]**. Unless SSM can fully pass on higher costs to consumers, inflation poses a greater threat to profitability than the potential benefits of increased employment **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Increase in employment**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Higher disposable incomes as more people are employed → increased sales of washing machines → higher demand for SSM soap powder
>     - Broader customer base with spending power → steadier revenue growth
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Greater competition for labour → wage rates may rise → higher production costs for SSM
>     - Recruitment challenges if new staff are hard to find → potential production delays
> - **Increase in inflation**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - If wage increases are matched by productivity gains → unit labour cost may remain stable
>     - Soap powder is a necessity → demand may stay resilient even as prices rise
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Rising raw-material costs → SSM may need to raise prices to protect margins → risk of reduced sales volume
>     - 8 % inflation → pressure to increase wages → further cost inflation
>     - Cheaper imports from countries with lower inflation → competitive pricing pressure on SSM
>     - Higher living costs → consumers may cut back on non-essential items if prices climb
> - **Conclusion**
> 
>   - The boost in employment can drive higher soap-powder sales, but SSM must manage rising wage pressures and recruitment risks
>   - Inflation threatens both input costs and consumer spending power, though necessity status and productivity gains can cushion the impact
>   - SSM should focus on cost controls (e.g. supplier contracts, efficiency) and value pricing to harness employment-led demand while offsetting inflationary challenges

**Extract:**

**Vegetable Palace (VP) **

VP was started 10 years ago in country Z. It is a public limited company. VP has a chain of 500 fast-food restaurants that operate across country Z. The VP brand is famous for its vegetarian food, this means none of its meals contain meat.

VP has a head office in Main City where all the directors and senior managers work. There are many barriers to communication. Each VP restaurant has a Manager, an Assistant Manager and 50 employees who cook and serve the meals. Restaurant Managers are often very busy and they are considering delegating some of their tasks to the Assistant Managers.

The ingredients for the restaurants are ordered in bulk by head office and then distributed from its warehouse to each of the restaurants. However, some senior managers think that Restaurant Managers should purchase their own ingredients from local suppliers. This would mean the ingredients would be fresher and would allow variations in the meals served.

VP wants to expand into another country. It will choose between the two countries shown in Appendix 2. VP will also need to decide how to enter a new market in another country. It has the option of forming a joint venture with another business or franchising the VP brand. The choice of finance will need to be considered for the expansion and the amount of finance will depend on the option chosen.

**Appendix 1 **

**Advertisement for VP's restaurants **

Choose VP for the finest vegetarian meals. Our service is the fastest possible!

You will receive your meal in less than 5 minutes – guaranteed!

**SunnyShade Hats (SSH)**

SunnyShade Hats is a private limited company (Ltd) that designs and makes sun hats. It started six years ago and now has 40 production workers and 8 office staff in City M. SSH sells hats on its website and to independent clothes shops. The owners, Naila and Amir, want to expand by launching a new eco-friendly range called OceanWave.

Quality is very important. Recent checks show defect rates have increased as new staff have joined. SSH plans to hire 20 more machinists. Managers are deciding how to motivate staff to increase output and reduce defects. Two ideas are:

- Piece rate (a payment per hat made)
- Job rotation with extra skills training

SSH is also reviewing its packaging for online orders. The current plastic mailer is cheap and waterproof. A supplier has offered recyclable cardboard packaging that looks premium but costs more and may be less water-resistant.

In terms of the weaker currency, SSH buys fabric in USD** [Ap]**, so the same dollar invoice converts into more local-currency. This raises variable cost per hat unless prices increase or suppliers renegotiate, squeezing margins just as OceanWave launches **[An]**

As a result of the minimum wage rise of 5%, labour costs for the forty (and, soon, twenty more) machinists would increase** [Ap]**, pushing unit costs up. parts.problemMd: Do you think businesses are more affected by pressure groups than by other stakeholder groups? **Justify** your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Businesses may be more affected by other stakeholder groups because shareholders have direct financial control over company decisions **[K]**. This gives them immediate power to influence strategic direction and operational priorities through voting rights and investment decisions **[An]**

However, pressure groups can mobilise widespread public campaigns and coordinate boycotts that significantly impact sales revenue **[K]**, as they can reach large consumer bases and create sustained negative publicity that damages brand reputation **[An]**

Businesses should recognise that whilst shareholders and employees have direct contractual relationships that create immediate operational pressures, pressure groups often represent broader societal concerns that can lead to regulatory changes and long-term market shifts **[E]**. Furthermore, companies that prioritise shareholder demands over pressure group concerns may achieve short-term financial gains but risk facing coordinated activism that can ultimately threaten their social licence to operate and sustainable profitability **[E]**

>

>   - Give a different possible reason or viewpoint → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this could also affect the business → 1 An mark

>

> 
>   - Shareholders control investment and dividend decisions [k] directly affecting company financing and strategic options [an]
>   - Employees can strike or reduce productivity [k] immediately disrupting operations and profitability [an]
>   - Customers make direct purchasing decisions [k] providing immediate revenue feedback on business actions [an]
>   - Pressure groups lack direct financial control [k] limiting their immediate operational impact [an]
>   - Pressure groups can coordinate large-scale campaigns [k] creating widespread reputational damage and consumer boycotts [an]
>   - Pressure groups influence government policy [k] leading to regulatory changes that affect entire industries [an]
>   - Other stakeholders have contractual relationships [k] giving them legal rights and immediate influence [an]
>

>   - No, other stakeholder groups like shareholders and employees have direct control mechanisms [k] that immediately affect business operations and decision-making [an].

**RMT Clothing Ltd**

RMT Clothing Ltd is a medium-sized clothing retailer based in Country X. It was founded in 1995 and has grown to 50 stores across the country, selling affordable fashion for men and women aged 18-35. RMT currently employs 800 people, and had annual revenue of \$85 million last year.

The company is facing increasing competition from online retailers. RMT's CEO, Sarah Jones, is considering whether to close 10 underperforming stores and invest in expanding the company's e-commerce operations instead. This would involve making 100 store staff redundant but hiring 50 new employees to work on the website and in the distribution centre.

RMT's financial performance over the last 3 years is shown in table 1 below.

**Table 1: RMT’s Financial Performance 2020 to 2022**

| Year | Revenue (\$m) | Profit (\$m) | Online sales (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2020 | 80 | 4.0 | 15 |
| 2021 | 82 | 3.8 | 18 |
| 2022 | 85 | 3.5 | 22 |

The company's main stakeholders have differing views on the proposed changes. Shareholders are concerned about falling profits and want to see a clear plan for growth. Employees are worried about potential job losses. Customers have been complaining that RMT's website is difficult to use compared to competitors.

RMT is also facing external challenges including rising energy and material costs, as well as changing consumer preferences towards more sustainable fashion. However, there are opportunities to expand into new international markets through e-commerce.

Sarah needs to decide on the best strategy to ensure RMT's long-term success in a rapidly changing retail environment.

Consider the potential responses of the following two pressure groups to RMT's proposed changes:

- Trade unions representing retail workers
- Local community groups in areas where stores may close

Analyse how each pressure group might respond to RMT's plans for redundancies and store closures. Which pressure group should RMT be most concerned about? **Justify** your answer.

Refer to the following [insert](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/10/rmt-clothing-ltd-case-study.pdf) when answering the question
parts.solutionMd:
Trade unions would likely oppose the redundancies strongly **[Ap]**, as protecting jobs is their primary purpose and 100 workers would lose employment **[An]**. They could organise strikes or industrial action to disrupt RMT's operations **[An]**, potentially damaging productivity and customer service during the transition period **[An]**. Trade unions might also launch negative publicity campaigns highlighting job losses **[Ap]**, which could harm RMT's brand reputation and customer loyalty **[An]**. However, unions might be willing to negotiate if RMT offers retraining for the 50 new e-commerce roles **[An]**.

Local community groups would be concerned about losing retail services in their areas **[Ap]**, as store closures reduce shopping convenience for residents **[An]**. They could organise boycotts of remaining RMT stores **[An]**, encouraging local customers to shop with competitors instead **[An]**. Community groups might lobby local councils to refuse planning permission for future RMT developments **[Ap]**, limiting the company's expansion opportunities **[An]**. However, their influence may be limited to specific geographical areas **[An]**.

I recommend RMT should be most concerned about trade unions **[E]**. While community groups affect local areas, trade unions have national influence and can disrupt operations across all RMT stores through coordinated action **[E]**. The timing is critical as RMT needs smooth operations during the transition to e-commerce **[Ap]**, and industrial action could delay the restructuring and worsen financial performance **[E]**. Trade unions also have stronger legal protections and established negotiation processes **[E]**, making them harder to ignore than community pressure groups **[E]**.

>

>

>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail about redundancies/closures
>   - Analysis (An): Explain potential responses and business impact
>   - Add a final Evaluation (E):
>   
>     - Decide which pressure group poses the greatest threat
>     - Justify your choice with business reasoning
>     - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts about job losses and store closures
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms for pressure group responses
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Trade unions representing retail workers**
> 
>   - **Potential responses**
>   
>     - Organise strikes and industrial action → disrupts operations and customer service
>     - Launch publicity campaigns against job losses → damages brand reputation
>     - Negotiate for better redundancy packages → increases restructuring costs
>     - Demand retraining opportunities for affected workers → may delay implementation
>   - **Concerns and impact**
>   
>     - 100 redundancies directly affect union members → strong motivation to resist
>     - National reach allows coordinated action across multiple stores → widespread disruption
>     - Legal rights to collective bargaining → cannot be easily dismissed
>     - Media support for workers' rights → amplifies negative publicity
> - **Local community groups**
> 
>   - **Potential responses**

>     - Lobby councils against future planning applications → limits expansion opportunities
>     - Campaign for alternative retailers to fill vacant premises → increases local competition
>     - Generate negative local media coverage → damages community relations
>   - **Concerns and impact**
>   
>     - Loss of local shopping convenience → affects community cohesion
>     - Reduced footfall in local shopping areas → impacts other businesses
>     - Limited to specific geographical areas → localised rather than national impact
>     - Less formal organisation → easier for RMT to manage individually
> - **Recommendation**
> 
>   - Trade unions pose the greater threat because they can coordinate national action affecting all RMT operations, not just closed stores
>   - Their legal rights and established negotiation processes make them harder to ignore than community groups
>   - Industrial action during the critical transition period could severely damage RMT's restructuring plans and financial recovery

parts.problemMd: **Explain **why liquidity and profitability are important to a business.
parts.solutionMd:
Liquidity is a signal that a business will be able to pay back its short-term debts **[K]**, such as money owed to suppliers, workers' wages or fixed costs, such as rent **[An]**. If a business does not pay these debts, it would likely fail very quickly **[An]**. Without inventory or raw materials, staff to produce output, or a location in which to produce, it would have nothing to sell and would cease trading **[An]**

Profitability measures how well profit is being made from sales or capital invested in the business **[K]**. A profitable business will have  funds to reinvest in the business, perhaps to be used to fund expansion **[An]**. It is, therefore, a measure of success and also of business potential, in which banks and investors are often very interested **[An]** as it demonstrates that a business can provide a return either on the capital investors put in, or shares bought **[An]**

>   - If the business becomes illiquid it may be forced to sell business assets to pay debts and will cease trading
> - Profitability:

>   - Measured by gross profit margin/profit margin/ROCE

**The BB Health Spa (BB)**

Bethany owns The BB Health Spa in Main City in country X. Economic growth has been high for the last few years. The government of country X wants this growth to continue so it has reduced income tax. However, it is also worried about inflation becoming a problem so it has increased interest rates.

The BB Health Spa is very busy and Bethany is considering taking on a partner to help manage the business and give her more free time. However, she has been a sole trader for 10 years and wants the business to stay small.

The customers of The BB Health Spa are people of all ages who are interested in their health. Bethany employs two qualified workers to provide the treatments for customers. Bethany herself also provides customers with treatments. In addition, she does all the administration such as ordering inventory, accounts and paying invoices when the spa is closed.

The BB Health Spa still uses the original treatment equipment which was purchased when the business started. Some spas nearby have the latest equipment but these spas charge much higher prices than The BB Health Spa. Bethany records all the financial transactions by filling in accounts books by hand. This takes her a long time. Customers book appointments using the telephone and Bethany later telephones them to remind them when an appointment is due.

**September**

**New equipment now available in many health spas to make skin look younger**

There have been a number of changes in technology for health spas which allow the treatments to be much more effective in making skin look younger. Many people are keen to try these treatments using the latest equipment to get younger looking skin. This equipment is very expensive for health spas to buy or lease.

The news of these treatments has appeared on social media sites and on mobile phone Apps leading to higher demand. ‘Some customers will pay high prices for such treatments’, said a local health spa owner who is keen to promote his health spa as being one of the first to use the new equipment.

There have also been developments in software which make customer bookings and accounts much easier, quicker and with fewer mistakes. Automatic text (sms) messages are used to remind customers of their appointments – so no need to miss an appointment again.

Look out for these changes in health spas near you!

Consider the weekly forecasts in Appendix 2 for the two additional services Bethany could choose:

- steam room.

parts.solutionMd:
The steam room option aligns with BB's existing services like sports therapies and yoga, and would attract 200 weekly customers, significantly increasing foot traffic. Its \$5 fee is accessible and matches BB's pricing strategy. The profit margin is high at 50% (\$500 profit from \$1000 revenue), and needs less specialised skills to operate, making staffing easier for Bethany

However, it has a higher equipment lease cost of \$400 per week compared to \$175 for hair cuts. Its installation might disrupt the spa's operations and there's a risk that not all 200 projected customers will use the service regularly, potentially affecting the forecasted revenue

The haircut option would generate more weekly profit (\$550 compared to \$500 for the steam room). It could attract new clients who might then use other spa services. The higher price of \$25 could be seen as adding a premium service to BB's range

However, haircuts would only attract 50 weekly customers, limiting foot traffic increase. The profit margin is lower at 44% (\$550 profit from \$1250 revenue), and it requires more specialised skills, which could complicate staffing and management for Bethany

Bethany should choose the steam room option. It aligns with BB's existing services and matches Bethany's wish to keep BB small and manageable. While haircuts offer slightly higher absolute profit, the steam room's higher profit margin, better fit with BB's brand and has the potential to attract more customers. These factors make it the better choice for sustainable growth and profitability

parts.solutionMd:
Liquidity has weakened as the current ratio fell from 2.1:1 in 2025 to 1.29:1 in 2026. In 2026, current assets totalled £310k compared to £240k of current liabilities, whereas in 2025 the gap was much larger (£340k vs £160k) **[Ap]**. This means SSH has less working capital available to cover short-term debts. Managers will face tougher decisions about paying suppliers or investing in new staff, as cash reserves are now lower. This increases the risk of liquidity problems, reducing flexibility in day-to-day decision-making** [An]**

Receivables have increased while cash has fallen. Trade receivables are £30k higher, while cash is £30k lower compared with 2025 **[Ap]**. More money is tied up in customers not yet paying, creating slower cash inflows **[K]**. This weakens liquidity further, meaning SSH may need to chase payments urgently or use the overdraft to fund operations. Managers may delay hiring or training decisions until cash becomes available, reducing the firm’s ability to expand quickly** [An]**

The business is also now reliant on an overdraft **[Ap]**. SSH took out a new £50k overdraft in 2026, alongside £30k higher payables **[Ap]**. The overdraft provides short-term relief for paying suppliers, but it adds interest costs. This makes decision-making riskier, as managers must balance the need for immediate liquidity with the long-term impact of higher expenses. If interest rates rise again, the cost of this decision could increase** [An]**

The most significant issue is the rise in receivables, as this directly slows down the inflow of cash needed for daily operations **[E]**. While the overdraft helps in the short term, it is only a temporary fix. Weakening liquidity ratios are concerning, but they are partly a result of the receivables problem. Therefore, tightening credit control and chasing payments should be the priority over alternatives such as delaying recruitment or packaging investment, as recovering cash will improve liquidity and decision-making flexibility **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Do you think issuing new shares is a better way for a limited company to finance expansion than using a bank loan? **Justify **your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Issuing new shares allows a limited company to raise large amounts of capital without taking on debt** [K]**. The company does not have to repay the money or pay interest, which helps keep costs down. However, issuing shares means giving up some ownership and control over decision making to new shareholders **[An]**

A bank loan provides a set amount of money that must be repaid with interest over time **[K]**. This increases the company's debt and financial risk. However, existing owners retain full control of the business. Loans can also be arranged relatively quickly and cheaply compared to issuing shares **[An]**

Overall, issuing new shares is likely the better option for financing expansion. While it reduces owner control, it provides more long-term financial flexibility than a loan **[E}**. The company avoids taking on debt and interest payments, allowing more profits to be reinvested for future growth. This makes shares more suitable for expansion plans **[E]**

The sources of finance for the business were \$10 000 of savings from each partner and a bank loan of \$10 000. CC was also given a government grant to help the new business get started. CC leased a factory, bought some equipment and had to pay some expenses before the business had regular cash inflows.

CC’s current product is a range of standardised phone covers which are sold in the mass market. These are sold using a competitive pricing method through mobile phone shops. CC employs 10 skilled production workers who are paid just above the legal minimum wage. These workers have been trained how to operate the equipment and work as a team on the production line. During the production process there is a lot of waste plastic produced and CC sends this to landfill sites. The business has just completed its second year of trading.

CC is about to launch a new range of individual personalised phone covers. It will need to recruit 2 additional production workers. Aruna knows that the marketing mix for this new product may have to be different to the marketing mix used for the standardised products. The new product will be aimed at a niche market of high income consumers between the ages of 18 to 25. There are few other competitors in this market at present.

**Appendix 1 **

**Newspaper article in Main News **

Country Z has been in a recession but the economy is now growing rapidly and unemployment is falling. With higher incomes the majority of people now own a mobile phone. This makes communication easier. Mobile banking is becoming more popular and it is used by a large percentage of the population.

**Appendix 2 **

**Advertisement for CC’s standardised mobile phone covers**

Do you want to protect your phone from damage? Then buy a phone cover from CC. Your phone will never be damaged if you use one of our high quality covers!!

We offer a range of standardised covers at competitive prices. The CC range has many different colours and designs so you will stand out from the crowd.

**Appendix 3 **

**Summary of CC’s financial information from the end of the second year of trading (\$)**

| Revenue | 800 000 |
|---|---|
| Cost of sales | 400 000 |
| Gross profit | 400 000 |
| Expenses | 250 000 |
| Profit | 150 000 |
| Current Assets | 20 000 |

| Current liabilities | 15 000 |

**Explain two** reasons why finance is needed by CC.

Refer to the following [insert](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/nov-2020-paper-22-case-study-v2---new.pdf) when answering the question.
parts.solutionMd:
CC needed finance to start up the business **[K]**. Aisha and Aruna needed \$30,000 initially, which came from \$10,000 of savings from each partner and a \$10,000 bank loan **[Ap]**. Start-up finance is required because CC had lots of costs to cover **[An]**, such as leasing a factory and buying production equipment, before they started making money **[An]**

Secondly, CC needs finance to expand **[K] **the business. CC is about to launch a new range of personalised phone covers. This will require hiring two more workers **[Ap]**. Expanding into new products costs money for things like developing the product, marketing it, and paying for extra staff **[An]**. Having finance allows CC to grow and take advantage of new opportunities in the phone cover market **[An]**

> **[case-study]**
> BikeFix is a mobile bicycle repair service in a large city. Demand is higher in spring and summer. The owner wants to buy an electric van to reach more customers at weekends. BikeFix currently advertises with leaflets and social media. The owner is considering dynamic pricing (higher prices at peak times). Two finance options are being considered: a bank loan or leasing the van.
> 
> **Table 2.1 – Extract from BikeFix cash flow forecast (first quarter) \$s**
> 
> |   | **January** | **February** | **March** |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Opening balance | 2 000 | 3 500 | 2 800 |
> | Cash inflows (sales) | 6 000 | 5 400 | 7 200 |
> | Cash outflows (wages, fuel, parts, ads) | 4 500 | 6 100 | 5 900 |
> | **Net cash flow** | **1 500** | **X** | **1 300** |
> | **Closing balance** | **3 500** | 2 800 | **Y** |

Which source of finance is likely to be better for BikeFix to buy the electric van?

- Bank loan
- Leasing

Justify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
With leasing there is a lower initial cash outlay **[K]**, which means BikeFix can keep cash for parts and advertising **[Ap]**, reducing liquidity risk while testing weekend demand before committing to an asset for the long term **[An]**. However, BikeFix would never own the van and there may be limits on mileage and how the van can be modified to carry, for example, tools **[Ap]**

With a loan, ownership of the asset appears on the balance sheet** [K]**, increasing the value of the business, and allows for long-term use without mileage limits **[Ap]**. As a result, total cost may be lower over the van’s life, improving profitability once demand is proven** [An]**

Overall, though, because demand is seasonal and still growing, leasing is better now to protect cash flow and match payments to use** [E]**. BikeFix can switch to ownership later when revenue is more stable** **and when the cost of purchasing could well be lower **[E] **

>     - Maintenance often included and it may be easier to upgrade as technology improves
>     - Matches payments to usage; useful while testing weekend demand
>   - Loan (ownership) – why it may be better
>   
>     - Asset owned; no mileage/condition penalties; resale value at the end

Her children are now at school, so Kaari decided to start her own business making wooden playground equipment. Kaari started PPE as a sole trader business three years ago in country Z. She wants an income from the business but also wants to spend time with her children. Kaari wants the business to remain small. However, if the business grows Kaari may need to change to another type of business organisation. Kaari carries out all the management roles in the business. Kaari uses job production to produce high quality, individually designed playground equipment. Kaari designs all the equipment herself and she employs 3 skilled workers to help her make the products. PPE currently makes both large and small items of playground equipment each week. Kaari uses cost-plus pricing as every item of playground equipment uses different quantities of raw materials. She sells small items of playground equipment to retailers and large items of playground equipment to the Government. There are many competitors in this market. Kaari plans to obtain new machinery which will cost \$20 000. She is considering using crowd-funding as this is one way to raise capital for new business investment. Other options include leasing the machinery or asking the bank for a loan. Kaari has developed a new unique product this year. There are no other similar products in the market. **Appendix 1** **Advertisement for PPE** Buy your playground equipment from us. At PPE we manufacture high quality playground equipment and have better designs than our competitors. All our equipment has been fully tested and is guaranteed to meet legal safety standards. We are the main supplier of playground equipment to the Government for public parks - so you know our equipment can be trusted! Contact us today for a price list. **Appendix 2** **Cost and revenue information for PPE in 2021** | | **Small item of playground**

**equipment** | **Large item of playground**

**equipment** | |---|---|---| | Average selling price | \$100 | \$1 000 | | Average cost of manufacture | \$25 | \$500 | | Output each week | 15 | 3 | **Appendix 3** **Newspaper article – Main News 1st October 2021** **Children need to get more exercise and play outside** Research suggests that playing outside helps children relax after school and improves their health. The Government in country Z has allocated \$10m to spend on improving children’s playgrounds in public places. This means there will be \$5 000 to spend on equipment for each public playground. Retailers have reported increasing demand for small items of playground equipment as parents want to have these products at home. This trend is expected to continue. Consider the advantages and disadvantages to PPE of using the following **three** sources of finance to obtain new machinery: - Crowd-funding - Bank loan - Leasing Which source should PPE choose? **Justify **your answer. parts.solutionMd:
Crowd-funding could test public reaction to Kaari's unique new playground equipment designs **[Ap]**, potentially attracting retailers and government customers. However, if PPE doesn't reach the \$20,000 goal **[Ap]**, all money must be returned. There's also a risk of competitors stealing ideas in this competitive market **[An]**

A bank loan would provide the full \$20,000 upfront, allowing immediate machinery purchase. PPE could repay over years as revenue increases from both large and small equipment production **[Ap]**. However, as a small sole trader **[Ap]**, PPE may face high interest rates, and Kaari might need to provide collateral, risking personal assets **[An]**

A bank loan seems most suitable for PPE **[E]**. It provides immediate access to machinery, increasing production capacity without exposing designs **[Ap]** to competitors **[E], **which may be the case with crowdfunding **[E]**.
